questions.q: Write the exact Python syntax to create: (a) an empty list, (b) a list of three integers, (c) a list containing an integer, a float, a string, and another list.
questions.a: (a) `[]` or `list()` (b) `[10, 20, 30]` (c) `[42, 3.14, 'hello', [1, 2]]`. A wrong answer like `{}` for empty list reveals confusion with dictionary syntax. Using parentheses `(1,2,3)` reveals confusion with tuple syntax. Omitting the inner brackets in (c) shows misunderstanding of nesting.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why a list is called "mutable" and "heterogeneous". Give a one-line code example that proves each property.
questions.a: Mutable: contents can be changed after creation without creating a new object. Example: `lst = [1,2]; lst[0] = 99` changes first element. Heterogeneous: elements can be of different data types. Example: `lst = [1, 'a', 2.5]`. A wrong answer that says "mutable means you can add elements" confuses mutability with dynamic sizing (which is a consequence). Saying "heterogeneous means it can hold many elements" confuses heterogeneity with capacity.

questions.q: Create a list `employee` to store: name "Priya", employee ID 2045, department "IT", and a list of three project codes `[101, 102, 103]`. Then write the statement to change the department to "R&D".
questions.a: `employee = ['Priya', 2045, 'IT', [101, 102, 103]]` followed by `employee[2] = 'R&D'`. Steps: 1) Identify four components, 2) Use square brackets with commas, 3) Nest project codes in inner brackets, 4) Use zero-based indexing (department is at index 2), 5) Assign new string. A wrong index like `employee[3]` shows indexing confusion; using `employee.department` shows attribute-access confusion.

questions.q: Analyze the following two lists and explain the structural difference: `listA = [1, 2, [3, 4], 5]` and `listB = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`. How many elements does each have? What is the data type of the third element in `listA`?
questions.a: `listA` has 4 elements (the nested list `[3,4]` is a single element at index 2). `listB` has 5 elements. The third element of `listA` (index 2) is of type `list`. A student answering 5 elements for `listA` flattens the nested list mentally, a common error when visualizing nested structures. Saying the third element is `int` or `3` ignores the container.

questions.q: Evaluate which data structure — list or string — is more appropriate for storing a DNA sequence "ATCGATCG" if you need to: (i) replace the third base with 'G', (ii) extract a subsequence from position 2 to 5. Justify your choice.
questions.a: List is more appropriate. Strings are immutable, so (i) would require creating a new string, while a list allows `dna[2] = 'G'` in-place. For (ii), both support slicing, but list slicing returns a list which can be further mutated. Choosing string shows failure to apply mutability requirement; choosing list but saying "strings don't support slicing" shows factual error.

questions.q: Design a list structure to represent a weekly timetable for a student. Each day has a list of periods, each period is a list containing [subject, teacher, room]. Create the list for Monday with 3 periods: Physics (Dr. Rao, Lab1), Chemistry (Ms. Singh, Room20), Mathematics (Mr. Das, Room15). Write the Python code.
questions.a: `monday = [['Physics', 'Dr. Rao', 'Lab1'], ['Chemistry', 'Ms. Singh', 'Room20'], ['Mathematics', 'Mr. Das', 'Room15']]`. A good answer uses three nested lists inside an outer list. A poor answer uses a flat list `['Physics', 'Dr. Rao', 'Lab1', 'Chemistry', ...]` losing the period grouping, or uses dictionaries (not yet taught), showing inability to map real-world hierarchy to nested lists.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A list in Python is an ordered, mutable sequence of elements enclosed in square brackets [] and separated by commas, where each element can be of any data type (integer, float, string, list, tuple, etc.) allowing ______ collections.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you need to store a student's complete record: name (string), roll number (integer), marks in five subjects (list of integers), and overall ______ (float).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently create lists with homogeneous and heterogeneous elements, create nested lists, explain the significance of mutability and ordering, and distinguish list syntax from strings and tuples using correct terminology.
